name: Hay
model: written by hand (Claude) from the Urdu KB

aspects.overview: Hay (dry fodder) can be made from berseem, lucerne, oats and different grasses. It can be fed in fodder-shortage periods and kept for a long time without losing its nutrition or smell. Demand is rising with the need for more milk and meat. In Punjab, rabi fodder (including hay crops) covered about 3.2 to 3.8 million acres in recent years; average yield was about 563 maunds per acre in 2019-20, 620 in 2020-21, 774 in 2021-22, 770 in 2022-23 and 758 in 2023-24. Yield can be raised with good land preparation, clean seed of recommended varieties, the right seed rate, timely sowing and rotating the fodder with other rabi crops. Frequent cutting also helps control weeds.
aspects.varieties: Use clean, healthy, weed-free seed of recommended varieties. Market seed often contains shaftal, chicory (kasni), riwari and onion-weed seed and weak seed, which lowers yield and quality. If seed has chicory mixed in, soak it in a 5 percent salt solution: the chicory seed floats and can be removed; then wash the seed well with plenty of water before sowing so germination isn't harmed. Seed is available from the Punjab Seed Corporation, the Fodder Research Institute Sargodha, the Regional Agricultural Research Institute Bahawalpur and the Fodder Research Station Faisalabad. The berseem variety Punjab Berseem is less affected by stem rot.
aspects.sowing: Prepare the land well, use clean seed of recommended varieties at the recommended seed rate, sow at the recommended time, and rotate with other crops. Follow the weather forecast, and drain extra water from fields after heavy rain.
aspects.harvesting:
Making hay: cut the fodder when flowering starts. Cut lucerne and berseem at about 10 percent flowering, when they are richest in nutrients. Leaves are more nutritious than stems, so choose leafy crops. Spread the cut fodder in rows to dry: it is ready in 2 to 3 days in summer and 5 to 6 days in winter. Finished hay should have 10 to 12 percent moisture. Machines can make bales, which are easy to protect from rain. Hay can be fed straight away, alone or mixed with green fodder.
Do not spray anything 20 to 25 days before cutting: sprayed fodder can harm the animals' health.
aspects.irrigation: In the seed crop, water as needed during flowering and pollination. Avoid over-watering, which encourages stem rot, and don't let water from a diseased field flow into healthy fields.
aspects.fertilizer: Use potash fertilizer and don't overuse nitrogen; if stem rot appears, cut back nitrogen.
aspects.pests_diseases:
Rule: never spray the crop meant for fodder. Spray only seed crops, or spray after cutting the fodder, in the morning or evening to protect bees. Nothing should be sprayed 20 to 25 days before cutting.
Armyworm (lashkari sundi): greenish-brown caterpillar with yellow stripes and two black spots behind the head; curls up when touched. From February–March it eats leaves down to the veins, plus flowers and buds. Don't spray full-grown caterpillars; wait until they pupate. Keep the crop weed-free, use light and sex-pheromone traps, and dig water-filled trenches with kerosene around badly hit fields so caterpillars can't move on. In severe attack, after cutting, spray per acre 50 ml flubendiamide, or 40 to 50 ml chlorantraniliprole, or 200 ml lufenuron.
American bollworm: eats leaves; hay crops suffer most. If essential, cut the fodder and then spray per acre 40 ml spinosad, or 25 ml flubendiamide, or 40 to 50 ml chlorantraniliprole, or 200 ml emamectin benzoate, or 200 ml lufenuron. Use light and pheromone traps; check seed crops and spray while caterpillars are young.
Looper (kubri sundi): green caterpillar that loops when moving; webs and eats tender leaves. Same rules: don't spray fodder, spray after cutting; trenches with kerosene around fields.
Whitefly (seed crop): sucks sap, leaves turn yellow with black sooty mould. Spray per acre 250 ml acetamiprid, or 400 ml flonicamid, or 500 ml pyriproxyfen.
Thrips (seed crop): suck sap so leaves dry. Spray 200 ml chlorfenapyr per acre, and use yellow or blue sticky traps.
Aphid (sust tela): dark green, sucks sap, sooty mould follows. Sow treated seed; never spray the fodder crop. On the seed crop spray per acre 200 ml imidacloprid or nitenpyram, or 250 ml acetamiprid or bifenthrin.
Shoot fly: enters and dries the shoots; in severe attack cut the fodder, then spray 200 ml imidacloprid or emamectin benzoate per acre.
Fodder weevil: larva and adult eat green leaf tissue and new shoots; cut the fodder early. On the seed crop spray 40 to 50 ml flubendiamide or chlorantraniliprole per acre.
Lygus and sting bugs: damage buds, flowers and green pods so flowers drop and seed shrivels, mostly in the seed crop. Spray a recommended insecticide.
Stem rot: use a lower seed rate, avoid over-watering, keep water from diseased fields away from healthy ones, rotate crops, use potash and don't overuse nitrogen. Punjab Berseem is less affected.
aspects.weeds:
Itsit: in early-sown crops spray pendimethalin 1.5 litres per acre three weeks to a month before sowing and irrigate; when the soil reaches workable moisture (wattar), plough and leave open.
Ghabbal grass in legume fodders (berseem, lucerne): spray quizalofop 350 to 400 ml per acre. Never use it on oats or ryegrass, which are grasses themselves.
Rotating with other rabi crops and frequent cutting also reduce weeds.
Do not hoe right after spraying: it breaks the weedicide layer and dust can carry the chemical into the farmer's body.

timing.sowing: rabi season, at the recommended time of the fodder crop used (berseem, lucerne, oats, grasses)
timing.harvesting: cut at the start of flowering (berseem and lucerne at about 10 percent bloom); dries in 2 to 3 days in summer, 5 to 6 in winter
